results.title: Columbia Pictures | UCLA Film & Television Archive
results.content: Throughout its history, Columbia produced films that reflected the social concerns of the day, beginning with Capra’s 1932 interracial love story, The Bitter Tea of General Yen (1933). Among the other films included in the UCLA Film & Television Archive’s collection are Blind Alley (1932), All the King's Men (1949), The Caine Mutiny (1954), On the Waterfront (1954), The Bridge On the River Kwai (1957), Porgy and Bess (1959), All the Young Men (1960), Guess Who’s Coming to Dinner? (1967), Five [...] (1967), Five Easy Pieces (1970), The Last Detail (1974) and The Big Chill (1983). [...] some of Columbia’s most prestigious productions. It was Capra who directed the studio’s first all-talking picture, The Donavan Affair, and won the studio’s first Oscar, for the comedy It Happened One Night (1934).

results.title: Columbia Pictures: A Historical Overview | PDF | Sony Pictures | Film Production Companies Of The United States
results.content:
Columbia Pictures was founded in 1919 as Cohn-Brandt-Cohn Film Sales and renamed Columbia Pictures in 1924. It was a minor Hollywood studio in its early years but grew more successful in the 1920s-1930s under director Frank Capra and stars like Jean Arthur and Cary Grant. In the 1940s, Rita Hayworth propelled the studio's fortunes. In the 1950s-1980s, Columbia produced many hit films and TV shows through its Screen Gems subsidiary.
